title: Comparison of Canopeo and Samplepoint for Measuring Green Canopy Cover in Forage Crops
author: Govindasamy, Mahawer, et al.
materials: Canopeo, a digital image-based software for canopy measurement, is developed by Oklahoma State University and this application is available for Android and iOS devices with no costs (http://www.canopeoapp.com). It is an automatic color threshold (ACT) deduction software and measures the green ground cover based on red to green (R/G), blue to green (B/G) and an overload green index (2G – R – B) [5]. Canopeo, estimates green crop cover by turning green cover to white, and bare land area to black pixels, thereby it produces the percent white-colored pixels in a given image [16]. Furthermore, the pixel categorization using red to green and blue-to-green ratios in Canopeo is proven as an effective method to separate green surface with non-green surface. SamplePoint is also a no-cost computer-based software (http://www.samplepoint.org) developed by Booth et al. [4]. It works based on manual pixel classification (MPC) and targets up to 225 crosshairs per image. This software can distinguish broadleaf, grasses, shrub, cactus, litter, soil, stone, rock, and unknown by manual pixel classification which is an added advantage of this software compared to Canopeo. Based on the percentage of manual pixels for green canopy cover, soil, stone, and rocks, it provides the percentage of crop cover per unit area. While analysing the images the SamplePoint software overlay 100 crosshairs in each image and classify the objects in the image based on manual identification. Depending on the number of crosshairs intersecting green canopy out of 100 crosshairs counts is used to calculate the green cover percentage in a particular area.

Regression analysis was performed on the percent canopy cover (green) data obtained from Canopeo, SamplePoint, and visual assessments using the Proc REG procedure in SAS (version 9.3, SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC). The significance of the slopes were determined at P = 0.05. Visual assessment method used as a check in this study, therefore we took average of four persons (replication) observation and used it for further analysis. Pearson correlation analyses were performed to check the relationship among Canopeo, SamplePoint, and visual assessments of canopy covers in individual crops using the Proc CORR procedure in Statistical Analytical System (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC). Regression plots were made in Sigma Plot (version 10, Systat Software, Inc., San Jose, California, USA). For both regression and correlation analysis, the percent canopy estimation of individual methods was used as a variable, for example in Fig. 5A, the percent canopy estimation of the visual assessment method was used as an X variable, and the percent canopy estimation of Canopeo as a Y variable. steps.title: Prepare field plots and sow seeds
steps.instruction: In Jhansi, India (25°29’48.4” N, 78°33’35.6” E, elevation 233 m), establish research plots for the following crops: corn (var. African tall), cowpea (var. Bundel Lobia 1), sorghum (var. MP Chari), Egyptian clover (var. Bundel berseem 2) and oats (var. JHO 822). Plant in June (rainy season onset) for the summer crops and in November for the winter crops. Use seed rates of 45 kg ha⁻¹ for corn, 40 kg ha⁻¹ for cowpea, 35 kg ha⁻¹ for sorghum, 25 kg ha⁻¹ for Egyptian clover and 90 kg ha⁻¹ for oats. Apply a row spacing of 40 cm for corn and 30 cm for cowpea and sorghum. Record average plant heights at the time of imaging (corn 85 cm, cowpea 48 cm, Egyptian clover 42 cm, oats 45 cm, sorghum 75 cm) and average leaf widths (corn 6.5 cm, cowpea 8.1 cm, Egyptian clover 4.5 cm, oats 1.8 cm, sorghum 3 cm). Apply fertilizers according to local recommended practices and soil‑test values.

steps.title: Set up camera stand
steps.instruction: Construct a camera stand from PVC pipes (see Fig. 1) that holds the camera at a fixed height of 1.5 m above the soil surface. Ensure the camera points directly downward (nadir, 90°) so that each image covers a 0.5 m² ground area.

steps.title: Capture nadir images
steps.instruction: Using a Canon SX710 HS digital camera (32 megapixel; minimum 20 MP required), capture images between 10 am and 2 pm on a cloud‑free sunny day. Record images when the crops are 45 days old. For each plot, randomly select three locations and take one nadir image per location, keeping the camera at the 1.5 m height. Save each image in JPEG format.

steps.title: Process images with Canopeo
steps.instruction: Open each JPEG image in the Canopeo app (Android/iOS, free). Set the software parameters to Red/Green ratio = 0.97, Blue/Green ratio = 0.97, and enable noise reduction (value = 1). Run the analysis; processing takes 1.5–2 min per image. Record the percentage of white pixels reported by Canopeo as the green canopy cover.

steps.title: Process images with SamplePoint
steps.instruction: Open each JPEG image in SamplePoint (free, http://www.samplepoint.org). Use the default overlay of 100 crosshairs (pixels). For each crosshair, manually classify the underlying object as green canopy, soil, stone, rock, etc. After classifying all 100 crosshairs, the software reports the percentage of crosshairs intersecting green canopy; record this value as the canopy cover. Processing takes about 1 min per image.

steps.title: Conduct visual canopy assessment
steps.instruction: Simultaneously with image capture, have four independent observers estimate the green canopy cover for each plot (visual assessment). Each observer records an estimate; the assessment takes > 2 min per observer. Compute the average of the four estimates and record it as the visual canopy cover.

steps.title: Perform statistical analysis
steps.instruction: Compile the percent canopy cover values from Canopeo, SamplePoint, and visual assessment for each plot. Using SAS version 9.3, run PROC REG to regress each method against the others; declare significance at P = 0.05. Use PROC CORR to calculate Pearson correlation coefficients among the three methods for each crop. Generate regression plots in SigmaPlot version 10. Record the following key results: linear relationship between Canopeo and visual assessment (R² = 0.96, p < 0.0001); linear relationship between SamplePoint and visual assessment (R² = 0.96, p < 0.0001); linear relationship between Canopeo and SamplePoint (R² = 0.98, p < 0.0001). Also note crop‑specific correlations (e.g., corn Canopeo vs visual R = ‑0.61, cowpea Canopeo vs visual R = 0.94, etc., as listed in Table 2).
